about: Data for solar-observatory.html. Live image URL patterns were read from the operators' own pages on 28 Sep 2026: sdo.gsfc.nasa.gov/data/ (AIA and HMI browse images, 48-hour movies at assets/img/latest/mpeg/latest_1024_<channel>.mp4), soho.nascom.nasa.gov/data/realtime-images.html (512 px) and the /data/realtime/<camera>/1024/ directory listing (1024 px latest.jpg), www.spaceweather.gov SUVI product page (services.swpc.noaa.gov animations), and api.helioviewer.org/v2/getDataSources/ (source ids) plus the takeScreenshot API reference. Channel temperatures: Lemen et al. (2012), Solar Physics 275, 17, Table 1, and sdo.gsfc.nasa.gov/data/channels.php (log T). Gallery items use the same schema as data/gallery.json and are also appended there with category 'Sun'.

channels.label: 171 Å
channels.name: Extreme ultraviolet 171 Å
channels.what: Golden arches of plasma trace the magnetic field lines that loop up out of active regions. The default view, because it shows the corona's magnetic skeleton most clearly.

channels.label: 193 Å
channels.name: Extreme ultraviolet 193 Å
channels.ion: Fe XII, and Fe XXIV in flares
channels.what: The best channel for coronal holes: the dark patches where the magnetic field opens into space and the fast solar wind escapes toward Earth.

channels.label: 211 Å
channels.name: Extreme ultraviolet 211 Å
channels.what: Hotter, magnetically active regions glow; the quiet Sun between them fades to violet haze.

channels.label: 335 Å
channels.name: Extreme ultraviolet 335 Å
channels.what: A faint channel that follows the hottest parts of active regions, useful for measuring how much plasma sits at each temperature.

channels.label: 94 Å
channels.name: Extreme ultraviolet 94 Å
channels.what: Mostly dark and grainy until something flares; then the hottest loops light up green.

channels.label: 131 Å
channels.name: Extreme ultraviolet 131 Å
channels.ion: Fe VIII, Fe XXI and Fe XXIII
channels.what: Sees two very different temperatures at once. The channel NASA uses for its dramatic flare pictures, where the flare core glows teal and white.

channels.label: 304 Å
channels.name: Extreme ultraviolet 304 Å
channels.what: Prominences and filaments: cooler, denser clouds held above the surface by magnetic fields. On the limb they arch into space; on the disk they look like dark threads.

channels.label: 1600 Å
channels.name: Far ultraviolet 1600 Å
channels.what: A bright network of magnetic field outlines the convection cells below; flare ribbons shine brightly here.

channels.label: 1700 Å
channels.name: Ultraviolet continuum 1700 Å
channels.what: The coolest layer of the solar atmosphere, just above the visible surface. Sunspots appear dark, bright plage around them.

channels.label: Visible
channels.name: Intensitygram (visible light, 6173 Å)
channels.what: The Sun as your eyes would see it through a safe filter: limb darkening at the edge and sunspots, many of them wider than Earth.

channels.label: Magnetic
channels.name: Magnetogram
channels.ion: Zeeman splitting of Fe I 6173 Å
channels.what: White is magnetic field pointing toward us (north polarity), black points away (south). Every sunspot group is a white-and-black pair, and each hemisphere's pairs lead with opposite colours: Hale's law.

channels.label: 3-colour
channels.name: Composite 211 + 193 + 171 Å
channels.ion: Fe XIV + Fe XII + Fe IX
channels.what: Red, green and blue each carry one channel, so colour itself becomes a thermometer: hotter active regions look pink-red, cooler loops blue-gold, coronal holes stay dark.

cams.name: LASCO C2
cams.text: An occulting disk held on a thin arm (the dark shape in the middle) blocks the blinding solar disk; the white circle drawn on it marks the Sun's true size. What remains is the faint outer corona: streamers, and Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs), billion-tonne clouds of plasma that expand as bright loops or, when aimed at Earth, as a ring all around the disk (a "halo CME").

cams.name: LASCO C3
cams.text: A wider view, about 30 solar diameters across. Background stars drift slowly from left to right as SOHO circles the Sun with Earth; bright planets appear with horizontal bars where they overfill the camera's pixels. Most of the more than 5,000 comets SOHO has discovered were spotted in C2 and C3 by volunteers in the Sungrazer Project.

channels.label: 94 Å
channels.text: Flare plasma near 6 million K. Mostly dark until a flare.

channels.label: 131 Å
channels.text: Flares at 10 million K, plus cooler transition-region gas.

channels.label: 195 Å
channels.text: The corona near 1.5 million K; coronal holes appear dark. NOAA's forecasters watch this one most.

channels.label: Thematic map
channels.text: Not a photograph: a classifier looks at all six channels at once and labels every pixel as a solar feature, such as coronal hole, filament, prominence, flare, bright region or quiet Sun (Hughes et al. 2019). Forecasters use it to find the features that drive space weather at a glance.

presets.label: Halloween storms
presets.text: 28 October 2003: an X17 flare, one of the largest ever recorded, bursts from a giant sunspot group. The Halloween storms that followed rerouted flights and damaged satellites. SDO did not exist yet, so this is SOHO's Extreme ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (EIT).

presets.label: Halloween CME
presets.text: The same morning in LASCO C2: a halo Coronal Mass Ejection racing straight at Earth, and a snowstorm of energetic particles hitting the camera.

presets.label: Bastille Day
presets.text: 14 July 2000: an X5.7 flare and Earth-directed CME, the 'Bastille Day event', which gave aurora as far south as Texas.

presets.label: Transit of Venus
presets.text: 6 June 2012: Venus crosses the face of the Sun, a dark round disk near the top of the image. The next transit of Venus is in December 2117.

presets.label: X9.3 flare
presets.text: 6 September 2017, 12:02 UTC: the most powerful flare of Solar Cycle 24 peaks in Active Region 12673, on the right of the disk.

presets.label: Solar minimum
presets.text: December 2019, the start of Solar Cycle 25: a blank, spotless Sun. Compare it with the maximum below.

presets.label: Eclipse day
presets.text: 8 April 2024, 18:40 UTC: the corona as SDO saw it at the moment totality reached Dallas, Texas. The streamers you could see by eye during the eclipse grow from these bright regions.

presets.label: Gannon storm
presets.text: 10 May 2024: the giant sunspot group of Active Region 13664, about 15 Earths across, just before the strongest geomagnetic storm in more than 20 years (named for solar physicist Jennifer Gannon). Aurora was seen from Mexico and Florida.

presets.label: AR 13664 in EUV
presets.text: 11 May 2024, 01:23 UTC: an X5.8 flare from the same region, one of a string of X-class flares it fired that week.

presets.label: Solar maximum
presets.text: August 2024, near the peak of Solar Cycle 25: the monthly sunspot number was the highest in 23 years.

presets.label: X9.0 flare
presets.text: 3 October 2024: an X9.0 flare, the strongest of Solar Cycle 25 so far.

gallery.title: Inouye's first look: the boiling surface
gallery.mission: Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST), Haleakalā, Maui
gallery.story: The first image from the 4-metre Inouye Solar Telescope, the largest solar telescope on Earth, shows a patch of the photosphere 36,500 km across. Each cell is a column of hot gas the size of Texas rising, cooling and sinking back in the dark lanes, where bright points mark bundles of magnetic field. Features as small as 30 km were seen for the first time.

gallery.title: A light bridge across a sunspot
gallery.story: A bright bridge of hot gas crosses the dark umbra of a sunspot from one side of its filamentary penumbra to the other. Light bridges are thought to signal that a spot has begun to decay and will eventually break apart. Released with a set of sunspot and quiet-Sun images to preview what the telescope would do during Solar Cycle 25.

gallery.title: Sunspots through a tunable filter
gallery.instrument: Visible Tunable Filter (VTF), sodium D line 588.9 nm
gallery.story: First light for the largest imaging spectro-polarimeter ever built, made by the Institute for Solar Physics (KIS) in Freiburg, Germany. Tuned to the sodium D line, it shows sunspots and their surroundings with each pixel just 10 km on the Sun. Stepping through the line lets scientists measure temperature, motion and magnetic field layer by layer.

gallery.title: Campfires on the Sun
gallery.credit: Solar Orbiter / EUI Team (ESA & NASA); CSL, IAS, MPS, PMOD/WRC, ROB, UCL/MSSL
gallery.story: Solar Orbiter's first images, taken 77 million km from the Sun, revealed miniature flares everywhere across the quiet Sun: 'campfires' millions of times smaller than the flares we see from Earth. Scientists are testing whether countless tiny events like these help heat the corona to over a million degrees.

gallery.title: The first look at the Sun's south pole
gallery.instrument: Polarimetric and Helioseismic Imager (PHI), EUI and SPICE
gallery.credit: ESA & NASA / Solar Orbiter / PHI, EUI & SPICE teams
gallery.story: Every telescope before had seen the Sun from near its equator. After a Venus flyby tilted its orbit 17 degrees in February 2025, Solar Orbiter looked down on the south pole for the first time in March 2025 and found the magnetic field there a messy mixture of both polarities, as expected near solar maximum when the Sun's poles flip.

gallery.title: Inside the Sun's atmosphere
gallery.instrument: Wide-field Imager for Parker Solar Probe (WISPR)
gallery.credit: NASA / Johns Hopkins APL / Naval Research Laboratory
gallery.story: On 24 December 2024 Parker Solar Probe passed just 6.1 million km from the solar surface, moving at about 690,000 km/h, the fastest human-made object ever. Its WISPR camera looked out sideways through the corona and saw streamers and Coronal Mass Ejections from the inside, including colliding CMEs, in the closest images of the Sun ever taken.

gallery.title: September 2017: the cycle's biggest flares
gallery.story: In one week Active Region 12673 fired an X9.3 flare on 6 September, the strongest of Solar Cycle 24, then an X8.2 flare on 10 September as it rotated onto the limb. High-frequency radio blackouts hit the sunlit side of Earth while hurricanes Irma and Maria battered the Caribbean, disrupting emergency communications.

gallery.title: Active Region 13664 and the Gannon storm
gallery.instrument: Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA), 171 Å, via Helioviewer
gallery.credit: NASA / SDO (AIA); rendered by the Helioviewer Project
gallery.story: The giant sunspot group AR 13664 launched a string of X-class flares and a series of Earth-directed Coronal Mass Ejections in May 2024. They arrived together on 10 May and drove the strongest geomagnetic storm since 2003, later named the Gannon storm, with aurora seen from Mexico, Florida and northern India. This image is rendered live from SDO data for 12:00 UTC that day.

gallery.title: An erupting prominence
gallery.story: A long prominence, a cloud of relatively cool, dense plasma suspended in the million-degree corona, lifts off the limb. In this ionised-helium line the gas is about 60,000 K; the whitest areas are the hottest. SOHO has watched the Sun almost continuously from the L1 point since 1996.

gallery.title: Comet Bradfield in the coronagraph
gallery.instrument: Large Angle and Spectrometric Coronagraph (LASCO) C3
gallery.story: With the Sun hidden behind the occulting disk, a comet with a bright head and a long white tail swings past on its way around the Sun. SOHO's coronagraphs have become the most prolific comet finder in history, with more than 5,000 discoveries, most of them by amateur volunteers.

gallery.title: A ring of X-rays
gallery.story: On 4 January 2011 Europe saw a partial eclipse, but from Hinode's orbit the Moon passed entirely inside the solar disk, an annular eclipse seen in X-rays. The Moon's dark silhouette sits against the multi-million-degree corona, whose brightest knots are active regions.

gallery.title: Baily's beads, Great American Eclipse
gallery.story: The last beads of sunlight shine through valleys on the Moon's edge seconds before totality, with the pink chromosphere and white corona appearing around the rim. The 21 August 2017 eclipse was the first total eclipse to cross the United States coast to coast since 1918.

gallery.title: Prominences at totality, 2024
gallery.story: With the Moon covering the photosphere, pink prominences of glowing hydrogen stand out around the edge of the black disk. Near solar maximum, the 8 April 2024 eclipse showed a corona full of streamers and an unusually bright show of prominences across Mexico, the United States and Canada.
